en: The Jātaka:
The Eighth Chapter, The Section on Kaccāyana (Aṭṭhakanipāta Kaccānivagga)
9. The Aṭṭhāna Jātaka “The Gaṅgā, the night-lily, the swan,
the conch-colored one, and the cuckoo;”
One might as well give a palm fruit from Jambudvīpa at that time,
when the hair of a tortoise [is spun into thread].
The cloak may be of three kinds:
the winter cloak,
or perhaps it might then be that very one.
When a watchtower has been well-constructed for the sake of mosquitoes,
being firm and unshakable,
Then indeed it might be so,
when a ladder has been well-constructed for those who possess horns.
Then indeed it would be for the purpose of ascending to heaven,
when one has climbed up the ladder.
Crows would devour the moon,
and they would even cast down Rāhu—
only then, indeed, would it truly be so.
When flies that wander in swarms, having drunk from a jar of liquor,
should settle upon burning coals, [they will surely die].
Then indeed it would be so:
when a donkey might possess lips like the *bimba* fruit and have a handsome face.
One would surely be skilled in dance and song at that time,
when crows and owls [sing together].
If they were to deliberate in private and take delight in one another,
then indeed it would be so at that time.
When a parasol made of lotus leaves might be more stable than one made of palm leaves for warding off the rain, [then it would be better].
Then indeed it would be so,
when the bird Kulaka [reaches] Mount Gandhamādana.
One might take it up with the tip of one's mouth and go away;
only then, indeed, would it truly be so.
When [one boards] a ship of the ocean—
“Suppose a servant were to take a sleeping man,
along with his bed and bedding, and depart;
would it not surely be so then?”
The Aṭṭhāna Jātaka, the ninth.
